passages.title: Passage 1
passages.instructions:
Questions 1–40

You should spend about 60 minutes on Questions 1–40, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Cognitive Bias in Judgement

A Cognitive biases are systematic deviations from normative models of reasoning that influence medical diagnoses, judicial verdicts, and financial trades. Psychologists catalogue anchoring, availability, and confirmation tendencies using controlled experiments with student and professional samples. While heuristics conserve attention under uncertainty, they can entrench errors when stakes are high and feedback is delayed. Organisational researchers argue that debiasing training must target environments, not merely individual awareness, because structural prompts shape choices more reliably than one-off workshops. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.

B Anchoring occurs when initial numbers skew subsequent estimates even when anchors are obviously arbitrary. Real estate agents shown random listing figures adjust valuations toward those anchors despite denying influence. Courts have observed similar patterns in damage awards following early demands. Debiasing strategies include considering opposite anchors and requiring written justification before final judgments. The author notes that professionals often express confidence in their objectivity while remaining measurably susceptible in double-blind audit studies replicated across continents. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

C Availability bias overweight vivid events such as plane crashes or sensational crimes, leading policymakers to overfund rare risks while neglecting chronic harms like hypertension. Media cycles amplify exemplars that are memorable yet unrepresentative. Statistical literacy programmes aim to temper intuitive fears with base-rate information, though emotional imagery can override numerical tutoring in immediate decisions. Public health communicators experiment with reframing messages to highlight routine dangers without inducing fatalism among audiences already sceptical of institutional expertise after prior scandals. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

D Confirmation bias drives selective search for evidence supporting prior beliefs, visible in partisan news consumption and scientific peer review when reviewers favour familiar theories. Blind annotation and preregistration of analysis plans reduce but do not eliminate directional filtering. Teams that institutionalise devil's advocate roles surface disconfirming data earlier in product development pipelines. The writer cautions that diversity of viewpoints helps only when dissent is psychologically safe; token inclusion without power sharing may worsen groupthink disguised as consensus. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.

E Algorithmic decision aids promise consistency yet can encode historical biases present in training data, reproducing disparities in lending and sentencing recommendations. Explainability tools expose feature weights, enabling auditors to challenge proxies for protected attributes. Human overrides remain common when outputs conflict with intuition, sometimes reintroducing bias under the label of professional discretion. Regulators debate whether to mandate human review for high-impact predictions or to restrict certain models altogether when validation across subgroups proves inadequate in prospective field trials. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

F Cross-cultural studies reveal that some biases intensify under collectivist norms prioritising harmony, whereas individualist settings may encourage overconfidence in personal judgments. Translation of laboratory tasks complicates comparisons because linguistic framing alters risk preferences. Developmental evidence shows children exhibit precursor patterns, suggesting partial innateness interacting with schooling. Longitudinal cohorts link adolescent susceptibility to later financial distress, motivating early curricula on probabilistic thinking integrated with mathematics education rather than standalone pop psychology modules. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

G Looking ahead, the author believes bias mitigation will blend institutional design, transparent algorithms, and humble professional culture. No checklist eliminates fallibility, yet checklists can slow impulsive errors in emergency rooms and cockpits. If organisations reward decisive certainty over calibrated doubt, training effects will decay rapidly. Sustainable improvement requires metrics that track decision quality over time, not merely attendance at diversity seminars that rarely measure downstream outcomes on hiring, lending, or clinical pathways. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.
